strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation failure in perturbation prediction: high global correlation can coexist with poor recovery of sparse, perturbation-specific effects. The emphasis on DEG-aware and perturbation-discrimination metrics is valuable.

The proposed combination of perturbation-conditioned biological context, non-DEG regularization, and response-aware representation alignment is intuitively motivated and potentially useful for unseen-perturbation prediction.
Evaluation covers two large public Perturb-seq datasets, several recent graph and non-graph baselines, effect-size-stratified analyses, ablations, and one pathway-level case study.

ADAPERT obtains meaningful gains over TxPert on K562, especially for DES@50/100, and generally improves DEG direction and effect-ranking metrics. The manuscript is visually polished and mostly easy to follow.
No material human-subject or deployment risk is apparent because the experiments use public molecular datasets; however, this is not explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The proposed subgraph mechanism is not technically well specified. Equation 12 applies Gumbel-Softmax over all nodes and then hard-thresholds the samples, but no straight-through estimator or other differentiable treatment of the threshold is given. Consequently, the claimed differentiable node selection does not follow from the formulation and may provide no gradient to the scoring network.

The selected object is not clearly a learned subgraph in the operational sense: node embeddings are first computed on the full graph, and the context in Equation 13 simply sums selected embeddings. No message passing over the induced subgraph or use of its selected edges is defined. Claims about reducing noise propagation through a compact subgraph are therefore insufficiently supported.

The central comparison does not isolate the source of improvement. ADAPERT receives explicit training-time DEG/non-DEG supervision, whereas it is unclear whether baselines receive equivalent supervision. There is no controlled comparison adding the proposed losses to a static-graph baseline, nor separate ablations for the alignment loss, semantic embeddings, learned selection versus random/topological selection, or full graph versus selected graph.

Differential-expression construction is inadequately specified. The statistical test, aggregation or pairing of unpaired control and perturbed cells, multiple-testing correction, and handling of biological versus cellular replicates are omitted. Using an uncorrected p<0.05 threshold across thousands of genes could label many null genes as DEGs. The notation alternates between individual-cell and mean profiles without explaining how differences are computed.

Definitions are internally inconsistent. The main text and Table 5 define effect-size groups using the fraction of genes with p<0.05, whereas Figure 8 says groups are tertiles of mean absolute differential expression and DEGs use an absolute-change threshold of 0.1. DES is described as top-k overlap in the tables but as overlap between FDR-thresholded significant sets in Appendix B, without defining DES@K. These inconsistencies undermine reproducibility and interpretation.

The evidence does not justify several broad claims. On RPE1, ADAPERT is worse than MorPH on PDS (0.663 versus 0.688), and its DES gains over TxPert are very small (0.244 versus 0.242 and 0.320 versus 0.314). Reported standard deviations across perturbations are very large, while seed-level variability and paired statistical tests are absent. The single HIRA pathway example is exploratory rather than broad biological validation.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper provides no code or availability statement and omits key ADAPERT architecture and training choices, including dimensions, optimizer, learning rate, number of layers, lambda_align, Gumbel temperature and schedule, threshold T, subgraph sizes, random seeds, DEG-test details, and selected hyperparameters. Appendix Table 8 only describes TxPert and unexpectedly includes a non-DEG Huber loss, creating further ambiguity about the baseline implementation.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess. The claim of identical procedures and computational budgets is unsupported by concrete budgets or complete search spaces, and some listed models, such as unconditioned scVI or standard CPA, do not naturally predict wholly unseen perturbation identities without additional design choices that are not explained.

Originality is moderate rather than high: mean/mode collapse is acknowledged in cited prior work, while conditional node scoring, Gumbel selection, DEG masking, Huber regularization, and cosine alignment are established components. The paper needs stronger controlled evidence that their particular integration yields benefits beyond privileged DEG supervision.

There is no substantive limitations section. The manuscript does not discuss dependence on STRING and proprietary/precomputed OpenAI-derived embeddings, incomplete gene-description coverage, sensitivity to erroneous DEG labels, computational scaling of scoring all graph nodes, or possible failure on perturbations absent from the graph. These are important limitations, although no major ethical violation is evident.

strengths: The paper identifies an important failure mode: global expression metrics can obscure poor recovery of sparse, perturbation-specific effects. Evaluating Pearson-Δ, perturbation discrimination, DEG recovery, effect direction, and pathway enrichment is directionally valuable.

The perturbation-conditioned use of graph and textual priors is a plausible idea, and the K562 results show potentially meaningful improvements over TxPert, including DES@50 from 0.220 to 0.263 and PDS from 0.665 to 0.711.
The experiments include two cell lines, unseen-perturbation splits, effect-size stratification, several knowledge-guided baselines, and partial ablations of the context and non-DEG loss.
No material ethical concern is apparent because the study uses public cell-line data and existing biological resources.
weaknesses: Soundness is undermined by an incompletely specified core mechanism. Nodes are selected by thresholding Gumbel-Softmax weights, but the threshold, sparsity control, inference procedure, and treatment of the nondifferentiable selected-node set are unspecified. Moreover, the final context is only a sum of node embeddings, so the claim that the learned representation captures a perturbation-specific subgraph is not adequately established.

The central mean-collapse account is insufficiently supported. Equation 4 alone does not show that MSE necessarily produces zero perturbation effects, and the paper provides only a single illustrative perturbation rather than systematic calibration, false-positive, effect-shrinkage, or comparison-to-mean-predictor analyses. Claims of causal relevance are also unsupported by the observational predictive evaluation.

DEG supervision is methodologically questionable. A gene with p≥0.05 is treated as truly non-responsive, although failure to reject does not establish a null effect, and the stated p<0.05 rule does not mention multiple-testing correction across thousands of genes. Penalizing all such genes toward zero may encode statistical power and sample-size artifacts rather than biology.

The experimental definitions are internally inconsistent. Effect-size groups are variously defined using p<0.05 DEG fractions, fixed percentage thresholds, tertiles of mean absolute differential expression, and an absolute-change threshold of 0.1. DES@50/100 is described as top-k overlap, while Appendix B defines DES using predicted significant-DEG sets at a fixed FDR without defining the @K variant. Figure 8's caption also describes stacked bars and histograms although the displayed plots are box and violin plots.

The empirical advantage is overstated. On RPE1, ADAPERT has worse PDS than MorPH (0.663 versus 0.688), while its gains over TxPert are small for Pearson-Δ (0.674 versus 0.655), DES@50 (0.244 versus 0.242), and DES@100 (0.320 versus 0.314). Reported standard deviations in Table 1 are across perturbations rather than independent runs, and most comparisons lack seeds, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests, so superiority is not convincingly demonstrated.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed contribution. Removing all context does not compare learned selection against the full static graph, a fixed local neighborhood, semantic embeddings alone, or random/parameter-matched selection. There is no clear ablation of the alignment loss. Consequently, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to adaptive subgraph extraction.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript supplies no code or exact split identities and omits key ADAPERT hyperparameters, selected configurations, optimizer details, random seeds, sampling threshold and temperature, λ_align, and exact architecture. Appendix Table 8 is labeled as a TxPert search space yet unexpectedly includes the proposed non-DEG Huber loss, while the text claims it covers every baseline. The main text says GPT-4o encodes descriptions, whereas the appendix says precomputed GenePT Ada/Model-3 embeddings are used, without identifying the actual variant.

The evaluation is limited to two cell lines from the same study and protocol, and the pathway analysis covers only one perturbation. There is no dedicated limitations discussion addressing reliance on STRING and proprietary text embeddings, incomplete graph/description coverage, uncertainty in DEG calls, or restricted cross-dataset and cross-context generalization. Overall, the idea has merit, but unresolved methodological, evidential, and reproducibility problems prevent others from reliably validating or building on the claimed contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The evaluation uses perturbation-level held-out splits on two sizable CRISPR datasets and includes global, discrimination, DEG-aware, direction, and pathway-level metrics. The ablations and effect-size stratification provide useful evidence that the context representation and non-DEG penalty contribute to performance.

Significance: Addressing mean-collapse and sparse response recovery is important for biological usefulness. On K562, ADAPERT improves over TxPert from 0.220 to 0.263 on DES@50 and from 0.205 to 0.252 on DES@100, while also improving Pearson-Δ and PDS.
Originality: Combining perturbation-conditioned graph selection with response-aware alignment and non-DEG regularization is a coherent, moderately novel synthesis tailored to unseen perturbations.

Presentation: The motivation and overall architecture are generally clear, and the paper contains informative ablations, sensitivity analysis, dataset statistics, metric definitions, and a pathway case study.
Ethics: The experiments use public datasets and biological annotations, with no evident human-subject or privacy concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several headline claims contradict the tables. ADAPERT is not best on every RPE1 metric: MorPH has higher PDS in Table 1 (0.688 versus 0.663), and CPA has higher DES@100 in Table 10 (0.337 versus 0.320). Some RPE1 gains over TxPert are also very small, without paired tests or confidence intervals establishing significance.

The central DEG evaluation is inconsistently specified. Table 2 describes DES@K as top-k overlap, whereas Appendix B defines DES using FDR-thresholded predicted and true sets without K. DEG and effect-size definitions also conflict: the main text and Table 5 use p<0.05 and percentage-based bins, while Figure 8's caption says tertiles of mean absolute expression and an absolute-change threshold of 0.1. These discrepancies undermine the main evidence about sparse signal recovery.

DEGs are defined with uncorrected p<0.05 in Equation 14, despite testing thousands of genes, and the manuscript does not identify the statistical test, sample unit, covariates, or multiple-testing procedure. Because DEG labels supervise two losses and define key metrics and strata, this is a material methodological omission.

The graph mechanism is underspecified and somewhat overstated. Equations 9–13 globally score nodes and sum selected node embeddings; they do not enforce connectivity to the perturbed gene, although the text repeatedly describes a local subgraph centered on it. The Gumbel threshold, temperature schedule, selected-node counts, aggregation normalization, and test-time sampling procedure are absent.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or availability statement is provided; ADAPERT's complete architecture, hyperparameters, seeds, run count, preprocessing, control-cell pairing, exact splits, and compute requirements are missing. Table 8 is labeled as a TxPert search space but includes method-specific non-DEG-loss and graph choices, leaving the tuning protocol unclear.

Reported uncertainty is inconsistent: Table 1's standard deviations are across test perturbations, Table 2 says multiple runs but omits their number, and Table 10 reports no uncertainty. There is no paired comparison across identical held-out perturbations, so the reliability of modest improvements cannot be assessed.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: GNN embeddings, semantic gene embeddings, Gumbel selection, DEG-aware supervision, and Huber regularization are established components. Comparisons isolating learned selection from simpler top-k semantic/graph retrieval or parameter-matched regularization baselines are missing.

The pathway validation covers only one perturbation. Its reported correlation is moderate (r=0.53), only 3 of 14 ground-truth-significant pathways are significant in both analyses, and the text inconsistently says that 9 were identified as significant. It therefore offers limited biological validation.

Presentation and limitations: There are numerous terminology and caption inconsistencies, including calling Figure 9 a graph-hop DEG-coverage analysis while its panels are labeled 'top-10/top-20 predicted genes.' The paper has no substantive limitations discussion, including dependence on STRING and proprietary OpenAI-derived embeddings, incomplete gene coverage, possible annotation leakage, limited cell-line scope, or risks of interpreting predictions as causal mechanisms. These issues require substantial clarification before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation failure in perturbation-response prediction: global correlation can obscure poor recovery of sparse, biologically relevant changes. The emphasis on DEG-aware and perturbation-discrimination metrics is valuable.

The evaluation is broad, covering four cell lines, hundreds of unseen perturbations per dataset, several strong baselines, effect-size stratification, two evaluation protocols, pathway analyses, and graph/source/threshold ablations.

The reported gains over TxPert are generally consistent in the unseen-perturbation experiments, particularly on K562: Table 9 reports Pearson-Δ 0.6200 versus 0.5879, Overlap@50 0.2607 versus 0.2426, and DE Spearman LFC 0.6745 versus 0.6552.
The perturbation-conditioned use of graph and text information is a sensible, moderately original combination of adaptive subgraph extraction with response-aware supervision.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes an appropriate caution that computational predictions require experimental validation before clinical or safety-critical use.
weaknesses: The central subgraph-learning mechanism is not technically sound as specified. Equations 11–13 normalize scores over all nodes, apply Gumbel-Softmax, hard-select nodes satisfying a threshold, and then sum their unweighted embeddings. The hard threshold and discrete set construction provide no gradient to the scoring network unless an unstated straight-through or soft relaxation is used. Thus the claimed differentiable node selection cannot be reproduced from the method.

The equations contradict the empirical description. Because the Gumbel-Softmax weights in Equation 12 sum to one, a threshold of 0.10 can select at most nine nodes, whereas Figure 24 reports 182–233 selected nodes at that threshold. The main method scores all graph nodes, while Figure 8 describes scoring neighbors in a k-hop neighborhood. These discrepancies leave the actual algorithm unclear and undermine the central adaptive-subgraph claim.

Definitions essential to training and evaluation are inconsistent. Equation 14 uses unadjusted p<0.05; Appendix A uses BH-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.05; Appendix D states a default of FDR<0.05 plus |LFC|>0.25; and Figure 6 uses an absolute expression-change threshold of 0.1. Effect-size groups are described variously as DEG-ratio ranges, tertiles of DEG count, and tertiles of mean absolute differential expression. Since DEG labels directly define two losses, metrics, and stratified analyses, this is a material soundness problem.

Several reported conclusions overstate or conflict with the tables. The text says ADAPERT is best on both main datasets, but in Table 1 its RPE1 PDS is 0.663 versus MORPH's 0.688. Dataset counts also change without adequate explanation: JURKAT has 448 test perturbations in Table 4 but 446 in Table 10, HEPG2 has 497 versus 496, and RPE1 has 464 versus 461. Main-table values also differ from appendix values. These inconsistencies weaken confidence in the evaluation pipeline.

The paper does not establish that the gains specifically resolve mean collapse. Figure 25 shows only modest improvements over TxPert—3.0% DEG weighted-MSE and 1.8% non-DEG weighted-MSE—and no direct comparison to an explicit mean predictor across the principal mean-collapse analyses. The proposed non-DEG loss itself further pushes most predicted effects toward zero, so stronger evidence is needed to distinguish genuine recovery of perturbation-specific signal from metric-targeted regularization.

The ablations do not fully isolate the contribution. The method combines semantic GenePT embeddings, graph context, DEG-derived non-response supervision, and DEG-derived alignment, but the main ablation omits the alignment loss and lacks a complete factorial comparison against an equally parameterized semantic-only model. It is therefore unclear how much improvement comes from adaptive subgraph extraction rather than privileged DEG supervision or text embeddings.

Statistical reporting is inadequate. Standard deviations are sometimes across test perturbations and sometimes described as across runs; the number of seeds is not stated; several table entries lack uncertainty; and no paired confidence intervals or significance tests support the relatively small improvements on some datasets and metrics.

Reproducibility is insufficient for acceptance: no code or configuration artifact is identified, and important details such as hidden dimensions, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch construction, random seeds, loss weights, Huber threshold, default selection threshold, exact semantic embedding variant, and baseline tuning budgets are absent. The manuscript also alternates between precomputed GenePT descriptions and GPT-4o-generated fallback descriptions without specifying the prompts or generated records.

The task is introduced as conditional single-cell generation, but most reported results concern mean perturbation profiles. The manuscript does not evaluate distributional fidelity, cell-to-cell heterogeneity, or calibration, so its claims about predicting single-cell responses and reducing experimental burden are broader than the evidence supports.

The impact discussion is reasonable but incomplete: it does not address biases and version dependence in STRING, NCBI, and language-model-derived annotations, or the reproducibility and provenance risks of generated gene descriptions. Overall, the extensive experiments are promising, but the unresolved algorithmic contradiction and inconsistent DEG/evaluation definitions prevent reliable verification or reuse.

strengths: The paper targets an important failure mode in perturbation prediction: high aggregate correlation can conceal poor recovery of biologically relevant differential expression. Reporting DEG-aware, discrimination, and pathway-level metrics is therefore valuable.
The perturbation-conditioned graph-context idea is intuitive and has some originality as a combination of STRING structure, semantic gene embeddings, and sparse context selection.

The evaluation spans four cell lines and includes useful analyses of graph source, graph density, fixed versus adaptive context, DEG thresholds, and perturbation effect size. The appendix is extensive, and several comparisons show consistent, albeit modest, improvements over TxPert.

The impact statement appropriately cautions that computational predictions require experimental validation and should not directly inform safety-critical or clinical decisions. No major research-ethics violation is apparent in the manuscript reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d8bbfad959a8475fba5483c90a1c43f7/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Soundness: the subgraph-selection equations are incompatible with the reported behavior. Equations 11–12 normalize node weights to sum to one, so fewer than ten nodes can have weight strictly above T=0.10. Figure 24 nevertheless reports selecting 38, 42, 182, and 233 nodes at that threshold. Moreover, thresholding the weights to form a discrete node set is not differentiable unless an estimator such as straight-through sampling is specified. This directly undermines the central claim of differentiable, learned subgraph extraction.

Soundness and fairness: ADAPERT receives ground-truth training-set DEG identities and effect sizes through both L_non and L_align, whereas the baselines apparently receive only the standard reconstruction target. The paper does not adequately isolate whether gains come from this extra response-derived supervision, semantic embeddings, or adaptive graph selection. There is no clear ablation of L_align, and the graphical ablations lack numerical results and uncertainty.

Experimental definitions conflict throughout the paper. DEGs are variously defined using unadjusted p<0.05 (Eq. 14), BH-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.05 (Appendix A), FDR<0.05 plus |LFC|>0.25 (Appendix D), or an absolute expression-change threshold of 0.1 (Figure 6). Effect-size groups are described both as DEG-count tertiles and as fixed <5%, 5–10%, and >10% bins. These discrepancies make the training targets and stratified results ambiguous.

The DES metric is not consistently defined. Tables 2–3 describe DES@50/@100 as top-k DEG overlap, while Eq. 27 defines DES using sets of statistically significant predicted and true genes without any k. It is consequently unclear what the central DEG-aware numbers measure or how predicted significance was computed.

Reported evaluation populations and results are inconsistent. RPE1 has 464 test perturbations in Table 4 but 461 in Table 12; JURKAT has 448 versus 446; HEPG2 has 497 versus 496. Main-table PDS values differ from their appendix counterparts, Table 3 claims mean ± standard deviation but displays neither, and some methods are evaluated on substantially fewer conditions. These issues weaken confidence that comparisons use identical examples and protocols.

The evidence does not establish statistical reliability. Most tables report variation across perturbations rather than independent training runs, the number of seeds is unspecified, and there are no confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Several gains over TxPert are small, and ADAPERT is not uniformly best—for example, TxPert wins JURKAT DE-Spearman and HEPG2 Overlap@50, while MORPH has higher RPE1 centroid accuracy.

The claim that ADAPERT mitigates mean collapse is stronger than the evidence. Figure 25 shows only a 3.0% versus 1.8% weighted-MSE improvement on DEGs versus non-DEGs, while unweighted improvements are essentially identical (4.6% versus 4.7%). A single illustrative scatterplot and these error summaries do not establish improved calibration or systematically reduced effect shrinkage.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential architecture dimensions, optimizer and schedule, batch construction, epochs, random seeds, values or selection procedures for lambda_non, lambda_align, delta, tau, and T, and exact executable split identifiers. The method section describes a simple averaging GNN while the appendix mentions a four-layer GATv2 with skip concatenation. It also alternates between GPT-4o-generated descriptions and fixed GenePT embeddings without specifying a deterministic fallback procedure. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

Presentation is polished visually but technically imprecise. The main text incorrectly says all four datasets are from Replogle et al., whereas the appendix says only K562 and RPE1 are; sources for JURKAT and HEPG2 are not clearly identified. The manuscript also shifts between cell-level profiles and perturbation-mean profiles without explaining training or aggregation, and graph sizes vary between the HVG-restricted 4,509-node graph and an 18.2K-node graph without reconciliation.

Significance and originality are limited by the unresolved protocol issues. Perturbation-conditioned graph attention, semantic embeddings, sparsification, and DEG-weighted supervision are individually familiar ideas; the contribution is primarily their combination. The reported improvements could be useful if validated, but the current description and evidence do not support reliable adoption.

Limitations are treated only superficially. The paper lacks a substantive limitations section addressing dependence on incomplete or biased STRING edges, semantic-embedding provenance, poor performance on some pathways, applicability beyond the examined cell lines, or the consequences of using response-derived DEG labels. The generic impact statement does not resolve these scientific limitations.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important failure mode in perturbation-response prediction—good aggregate accuracy despite poor recovery of sparse, biologically relevant changes—and evaluates both global and DEG-focused behavior.
Originality: Combining perturbation-conditioned graph selection, semantic gene embeddings, non-DEG regularization, and DEG-driven representation alignment is a useful and reasonably novel synthesis.

Soundness/evidence: The evaluation is unusually broad, covering four cell lines, strong recent baselines, multiple metric families, graph variants, effect-size analyses, and pathway-level case studies. ADAPERT generally improves over TxPert in the within-cell-line unseen-perturbation experiments, including Pearson-delta and several DEG metrics.
Presentation: The motivation and high-level architecture are clear, and the figures, tables, and extensive appendix make the empirical story easy to follow visually.
Ethics: The impact statement appropriately cautions that computational predictions require experimental validation and should not directly support safety-critical or clinical decisions.
weaknesses: Soundness: The stated subgraph-selection mathematics is inconsistent with the reported behavior. Equations 11–12 normalize node weights with a global softmax, so at threshold T=0.10 fewer than 10 nodes can exceed the threshold, yet Figure 24 reports 42–233 selected nodes. Moreover, hard thresholding is not differentiable, and no straight-through estimator is specified. This prevents verification of the central method from the manuscript.

Soundness: The paper claims that the DEG-alignment loss makes selected subgraphs response-specific, but both the target projection and context representation are learned jointly with only a positive cosine-alignment objective; a shared representation can satisfy this objective without encoding perturbation-specific information. No ablation isolates L_align, and no quantitative analysis shows that selected genes actually correspond to relevant DEGs or pathways.

Evaluation definitions conflict materially. The main text defines DEGs using q<0.05, Appendix A uses BH-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.05, Appendix D states a default |LFC|>0.25, and Figure 6 uses an absolute-change threshold of 0.1. Likewise, effect-size groups are variously described as fixed DEG percentages, DEG-count tertiles, and tertiles of mean absolute differential expression. These inconsistencies undermine the central small-effect and mean-collapse analyses.

Some conclusions overstate the tables. Table 1 says ADAPERT has the best performance on both datasets, although MORPH has higher RPE1 PDS (0.688 versus 0.663). In the cross-cell-line study, ADAPERT is below Linear-GenePT and Perturb Mean on several metrics, while the separate Systema evaluation uses a substantially different number of K562 conditions without adequately reconciling the protocols.

Statistical support is insufficient. Table 1 reports variability across perturbations rather than independent training runs, Table 2 inconsistently omits standard deviations for some metrics, and no seed-level confidence intervals or paired significance tests establish that the often modest gains over TxPert are robust. Baselines are also evaluated on differing numbers of conditions in several appendix tables.

Reproducibility is inadequate: optimizer and scheduling details, epochs, batch sizes, seeds, architecture dimensions, loss weights, Huber threshold, Gumbel temperature schedule, selection implementation, and model-selection procedure are largely absent. The manuscript also provides no code or artifact statement and ambiguously alternates between precomputed GenePT embeddings and GPT-4o-generated descriptions without documenting prompts, versions, or caching.

Presentation and limitations: Metric names and definitions are inconsistent—DES@K is described as top-k overlap in the main text but defined through significance-thresholded DEG sets in Equation 27. Dataset counts also vary across tables. A dedicated limitations discussion is missing, particularly regarding dependence on STRING/GenePT coverage, potential leakage from literature-derived embeddings, external API reproducibility, and the gap between predictive association and causal biological interpretation.
